## The decision this serves

A reviewer asks which cells express your marker. You have Visium data. Decide whether that
sentence is available to you before you write the rebuttal.

::: {.callout-important}
**Scale.** Runs in about 2 min, peak memory under 2 GB. Nothing here stops being safe at
size — this lesson is about what the numbers mean, not how many of them there are.
:::

## Concept

Every spatial platform answers the same question — where in the tissue is this RNA — and
they split into two families that answer it by different physics. The family determines what
a row of your matrix is, and that determines which sentences you are allowed to write.

### Family one: capture-based

Tissue is placed on a slide carrying spatially barcoded oligonucleotides, permeabilised, and
mRNA diffuses down onto the barcoded surface where reverse transcription attaches a
positional barcode. The library is then sequenced conventionally. Position comes from the
barcode, not from an image.

So **resolution is a property of the array, not of the biology**. A Visium v1 capture area
is 6.5 × 6.5 mm holding 4,992 spots, each 55 µm in diameter, arranged in a honeycomb with
100 µm centre-to-centre spacing [@visium_spatialone_2024]; an 11 × 11 mm capture area holds
roughly 14,000.

Two consequences follow directly from that geometry, and both matter more than people
expect.

**You are not measuring most of the tissue.** Spot area times spot count over capture area
gives roughly 30% coverage — about **70% of the section is never sampled at all**
[@spot_deconvolution_cells_per_spot]. The gaps between spots contribute nothing, and your
eye interpolates across them without being asked.

**A spot is several cells, and how many depends on your tissue.** Simulation against real
tissue geometry gives median cells per 55 µm spot of **19 in mouse kidney, 6 in mouse
cortex, 5 in hippocampus, and 6 in human breast cancer**
[@spot_deconvolution_cells_per_spot]. The commonly quoted "1 to 10 cells" is optimistic for
dense tissue. Look up your own tissue rather than repeating a range.

Visium HD changes the geometry rather than the chemistry: a continuous lawn of 2 × 2 µm
barcoded squares with no gaps, conventionally binned to 8 × 8 µm for analysis
[@tenx_visium_hd_technote]. Two microns is smaller than a cell, which sounds like it solves
the problem. It does not, and the reason matters: **a bin is not a cell either.** A grid
square straddles boundaries arbitrarily and a cell spans several bins. You have traded "one
row is several cells" for "one row is part of a cell, and which part is decided by where the
grid happened to fall." Getting from bins to cells requires segmentation — lesson 7.

What you gain from this family is the whole transcriptome. You did not choose genes in
advance, so you can ask questions you had not thought of.

### Family two: imaging-based

No sequencing. Probes hybridise to transcripts in intact tissue and are read out optically
over multiple rounds, each transcript species carrying a codeword — a pattern of which
rounds it lights up in. Xenium builds signal by rolling circle amplification; MERFISH uses
combinatorial barcoding with error-robust codes; CosMx uses cyclic hybridisation. Details
differ, logic is shared.

Here resolution is diffraction-limited rather than array-limited. You get a point cloud of
molecules with coordinates, a morphology image, and **no cells at all** until someone draws
boundaries.

The cost is that you only measure the panel, and the constraint is physical rather than
commercial: transcripts are point sources in a diffraction-limited image, so as density
rises they overlap and become unresolvable. This is why panels are curated rather than
maximal and why very abundant transcripts are often excluded.

**Sensitivity runs opposite to intuition.** Benchmarking found Xenium's detection efficiency
to be **1.2 to 1.5 times that of Chromium v2 scRNA-seq**, depending on metric and region,
with commercial platforms converging on similar detection efficiency
[@xenium_quality_2025]. An imaging dataset is simultaneously *more* sensitive than your
scRNA-seq for the genes it measures and *blind* to everything else.

Platforms differ in noise as much as in sensitivity, and the differences are not small.
Systematic benchmarking across a tumour tissue microarray found Xenium with the lowest false
discovery rate in 15 of 22 tissue–cancer combinations, while CosMx detected more genes on a
substantially larger panel [@ist_benchmark_2025]. That work also found large shifts between
2023 and 2024 chemistry and algorithm versions — so any platform comparison you read is a
snapshot, including this one.

### The three regimes, and what each licenses

The whole lesson in one table. Before writing any sentence about your data, find your row.

| | **Spot** | **Bin** | **Cell** |
|---|---|---|---|
| Example | Visium v1/v2 | Visium HD 8 µm | Xenium, MERFISH, CosMx |
| One row is | a 55 µm disc | a grid square | a segmented region |
| Cells per row | 5–19, tissue-dependent | a fraction of one | one, if segmentation is right |
| Genes | whole transcriptome | whole transcriptome | panel only |
| Tissue sampled | ~30% | continuous | continuous |
| "This cell expresses X" | **no** | **no** | conditional on lesson 7 |
| "X and Y are co-expressed" | **no** — may be different cells | **no** | conditional on lesson 7 |
| "This region expresses X" | yes | yes | yes |

The rows marked no are where most published errors live. A spot with high *CD8A* and high
*PDCD1* tells you both are present in that 55 µm disc holding perhaps six cells. It does not
tell you one T cell expresses both, and no downstream analysis creates that information —
deconvolution returns proportions, not cells, which is lesson 8.

### Units, and the comparison that is never valid

Counts per spot, per bin and per cell are three quantities and none converts into another.
Spot counts scale with tissue on the spot; bin counts with bin area; cell counts with cell
volume in the section plane, and therefore with section thickness — lesson 2.

The trap: total counts per cell in a Xenium run are far lower than in scRNA-seq, and this is
routinely misread as poor quality. It is not. You are counting a few hundred panel genes
rather than twenty thousand, and per-panel-gene sensitivity is typically *higher* than
droplet scRNA-seq [@xenium_quality_2025]. Normalising a targeted dataset by total counts and
comparing to an untargeted one compares two different denominators.

**The assumption that breaks first.** That a row of the matrix corresponds to one cell.
Everything downstream treats rows as units of biology, and in two of the three regimes they
are not.

## Runnable notebook

The same tissue read in three regimes, with row semantics made explicit.

Data tier: **Committed toy**

::: {.callout-warning}
**Not yet executed.** No output shown and nothing cached.
:::

```{python}
#| label: regimes
import spatialdata as sd
import numpy as np

regimes = []
for label, path, table in [
    ("Visium (spot)",   "toy_visium.zarr",    "square_002um"),
    ("Visium HD (bin)", "toy_visium_hd.zarr", "square_008um"),
    ("Xenium (cell)",   "toy_xenium.zarr",    "table"),
]:
    sdata = sd.read_zarr(f"data/cache/{path}")
    t = sdata.tables[table]
    area_mm2 = np.prod(np.ptp(t.obsm["spatial"], axis=0)) / 1e6
    regimes.append((label, t, area_mm2))
    print(f"{label:<18} rows={t.n_obs:>7,}  genes={t.n_vars:>6,}  "
          f"rows/mm²={t.n_obs / area_mm2:>8.0f}  median counts={np.median(t.X.sum(1)):>6.0f}")
```

```{python}
#| label: assert-regimes
# Rows per unit area must differ by orders of magnitude across regimes.
# If they do not, two of these objects are the same regime and the lesson is lying.

density = {label: t.n_obs / area for label, t, area in regimes}

assert (density["Visium (spot)"] < density["Visium HD (bin)"]
        < density["Xenium (cell)"]), f"regimes not ordered by density: {density}"

# Visium geometry is fixed and known: ~100 spots per mm² on a 100 µm grid.
assert 80 < density["Visium (spot)"] < 120, (
    f"spot density {density['Visium (spot)']:.0f}/mm² is inconsistent with a "
    "100 µm centre-to-centre array; check the coordinate units (lesson 6)"
)

# Targeted versus untargeted, asserted rather than assumed.
assert regimes[2][1].n_vars < 1000 < regimes[0][1].n_vars
```

That second assert is worth noticing: because the Visium array geometry is fixed and
published, spot density per mm² is a quantity you can check against a specification. If it
comes back at 10,000 rather than ~100, your coordinates are in pixels rather than microns —
which is lesson 6, caught here for free.

## Rosetta panel

Reading each regime in R, and where the object model stops distinguishing them. A `Seurat`
object holds spots, bins and cells in the same slot, so the regime is carried in your head
rather than in the data structure.

```r
library(Seurat)

visium <- Load10X_Spatial("data/cache/toy_visium/")
xenium <- LoadXenium("data/cache/toy_xenium/")

ncol(visium)   # spots
ncol(xenium)   # cells

# Nothing in the object stops you writing this, which is the problem:
# FetchData(visium, c("CD8A", "PDCD1"))  ->  co-expression that may be six cells
```

## Failure mode

**What it produces.** The sentence "this cell type expresses X" written from spot data. The
analysis runs, the figure looks like every other figure, and the claim was never measurable.
Its commoner disguise: a spot-level correlation between two genes reported as
co-expression, when the genes sit in different cells sharing a 55 µm disc.

**The diagnostic that catches it.** Count nuclei per spot from the paired H&E or DAPI image
and report the median. Published estimates run from 5 to 19 depending on tissue
[@spot_deconvolution_cells_per_spot], so the number is never 1. Do this once per dataset,
put it in your methods, and an entire class of reviewer objection is foreclosed.

## Self-check

### Question 1

What is one row of your table?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

For Visium, a 55 µm disc containing a tissue-dependent mixture — median 19 cells in mouse
kidney, 5 to 6 in brain and breast [@spot_deconvolution_cells_per_spot]. For Visium HD, a
grid square whose boundary has no relationship to any cell boundary. For an imaging
platform, whatever the segmentation algorithm decided was a cell — a claim, not a
measurement.

Only the third can ever be a cell, and only if lesson 7 went well.
:::

### Question 2

Two genes correlate strongly across your Visium spots. What are the possible explanations?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

At least four, and the data cannot separate them. They may be co-expressed in the same
cells. They may sit in two different cell types that reliably co-occur in the same
neighbourhood. One may be expressed in a cell type whose abundance varies across the
section, dragging both signals with it. Or both may track a technical gradient in capture
efficiency — lesson 2.

Spot-level correlation is a statement about tissue composition, not transcriptional
regulation. Getting to the latter needs a cell-resolution platform or an orthogonal
experiment.
:::

### Question 3

Your Xenium cells have a median of 300 counts and a colleague calls it low quality next to
their scRNA-seq at 5,000. Are they right?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

No, because the denominators differ. Those 300 counts come from a panel of a few hundred
genes; the 5,000 from twenty thousand. Per gene, Xenium's detection efficiency has been
measured at 1.2–1.5× Chromium v2 [@xenium_quality_2025].

The right comparison is per-gene detection for genes present in both, ideally on matched
tissue. The wrong one — total counts — makes every targeted platform look broken forever.
:::

## Going further

Deconvolution, which recovers cell-type proportions within a spot, is lesson 8.
Segmentation, which decides what a cell is on imaging platforms, is lesson 7.

Deliberately omitted: which platform to buy. It depends on tissue, question and budget, and
the benchmarks themselves show large shifts between chemistry versions
[@ist_benchmark_2025] — so any recommendation here would expire before you read it.
